title: In 741 OpenNeuro fMRI studies, connectivity is mostly person-specific once 10 s are trimmed from each run end, but tSNR, DVARS and local voxel correlation are study-specific
abstract: After we removed the first and last 10 s of each run, connectivity between brain regions varied more between people in a study than between studies, in 741 OpenNeuro fMRI studies; signal-quality measures (tSNR, DVARS, local voxel correlation) varied mostly between studies. This tells which fMRI measures a meta-analysis or a pooled analysis of open data can compare between studies. We used minimally preprocessed ReadyNeuro data (4 people per study, up to 2 runs each) and 28 measures of connectivity, signal amplitude and signal timescale. For each measure we estimated the study share (the fraction of the total variance that is between studies) with a nested random-effects model. We set tests in 314 discovery studies and ran them in 403 held-out studies. On untrimmed runs the pre-registered tests passed, and raw connectivity looked study-dominated (study share of global connectivity 0.60; median over 7,021 edges 0.49). An independent review then showed that this came mostly from a brain-wide transient at the start of 18% of runs (very probably volumes recorded before steady state; about half of GE-scanner runs) and from run-end artifacts in a few studies. With 10 s trimmed at each end, the study share of global connectivity was 0.19, 0.17 and 0.11 in the discovery, held-out and 24 fresh validation studies (person share 0.53, 0.48, 0.70), and the person share exceeded the study share in 99%, 99% and 94% of edges. We pre-registered four validation tests after the review; all passed, including the two that react to trimming. In contrast, cortical tSNR (0.69-0.75), DVARS (0.88-0.89) and the correlation of neighbouring voxels (0.91-0.95) stayed mostly study-specific; the 1-s autocorrelation did too (0.89-0.94), but only 0.50-0.70 within one TR, because ReadyNeuro interpolates to 1 s frames. A metadata and data-quality model fit in discovery predicted 82% of the held-out study variance of the 1-s autocorrelation and 77% of DVARS (mainly TR) and 63% of the neighbour correlation (mainly voxel size). Network segregation kept a study share of 0.28-0.43 that the few available covariates did not predict. Limitations: one pipeline, no motion traces, 4 people per study, approximate intervals, some accessions that share people, and a study effect that mixes scanner, protocol, population and task.

display.caption: Share of the variance of 28 fMRI measures between studies (blue), between people in a study (orange) and between runs of a person (green), with 10 s trimmed at each run end. Bars: 314 discovery studies, with approximate 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals. Diamonds: 403 held-out studies; black squares: 24 fresh validation studies; red circles: held-out studies without trimming. Starred measures are voxel summaries of full runs.

(a) Variance components of global connectivity, raw and after white-matter/CSF regression, with and without trimming 10 s at each run end (left bar discovery, right bar held-out). (b) Median and IQR over 7,021 edges of the study share (blue) and person share (orange). (c) Study share of the voxel autocorrelation at 1-8 s in all studies and within TR strata.

(a) Cortex-mean signal in the first 90 s of the runs, averaged per study, by scanner vendor (solid: discovery; dashed: confirmation; band: SE over studies). GE studies start with a large brain-wide transient. (b) Between-study variance of global connectivity with all frames and with the first 30 s removed.
